_comment: Phase configuration is DATA, not code. Retuning which model runs which phase,
or what a phase is allowed to touch, must never require editing bin/spec-run.
Fields:
id             phase name, used on the CLI (--stop-after, --gate, --with)
skill          the speckit skill invoked as a slash command in the phase process
model          opus | sonnet | haiku | fable (a CLI alias, resolved at run time)
effort         low | medium | high | xhigh | max
artifact       file (relative to the feature dir) whose state is the ONLY
authority on whether the phase succeeded. null = no artifact,
verification is skipped and recorded as unevaluated.
max_budget_usd hard ceiling passed to --max-budget-usd. OMITTED here, on
purpose: no phase ships with a dollar ceiling, because a
ceiling that halts a phase mid-artifact costs more than it
saves. A truncated plan.md still verifies as present, and the
tasks phase then plans against it. max_turns is the backstop,
and it is always set. Add the key back per phase (or via
--config / SPEC_RUN_CONFIG) if you want a spend ceiling.
max_turns      hard ceiling passed to --max-turns. The real safety rail: it
bounds a runaway loop, which is the failure a ceiling should
catch, and it does not depend on how spend is metered.
SIZE IT FOR THE REPO, not for comfort. implement was 400 and
that was too small on a large monorepo: one phase ran over 70
MINUTES of productive, non-looping work (spec-first edits,
targeted single-file spec runs, type-checks between steps) and
was a third of the way through its task list. A cap hit by
honest work is not a safety rail, it is a truncation — and it
lands mid-task, which is the expensive place to stop.
⚠️ Sized on WALL CLOCK and task progress, deliberately, because
turn consumption cannot be observed while a phase runs: the CLI
reports num_turns only in its final result, and counting
assistant messages in the session transcript is NOT the same
quantity — a transcript showing 414 messages belonged to a phase
the CLI had not yet stopped at a 400 cap. So 1200 is headroom,
not a measured multiple. If a phase reaches it, suspect a loop
and read the transcript rather than raising it again.
gate           always | on_needs_input | never
optional       true = only runs when named in --with
deny_tools     added to defaults.deny_tools for this phase
write_scope    path prefixes this phase may modify. null = unrestricted.
Enforced AFTER the phase by comparing git status, because a
detected escape is verifiable where a path-scoped tool deny is not.
takes_description  true = the feature description is passed as the skill argument
chunked        true = run this phase REPEATEDLY, a fresh process each pass,
until tasks.md has no unchecked boxes. Only implement sets it.
Cost is ~linear in cache_read, which is ~98% of a phase's
input and grows with turn count, so a phase of T turns costs
roughly 90k*T + 0.7k*T^2 tokens. Splitting into k passes
leaves the linear term and divides the quadratic one by k —
measured ~3x on a ~600-turn implement. Requires that the
phase tick tasks AS IT GOES (see handoff_extra), because a
pass resumes from tasks.md and nothing else.
max_passes     ceiling on chunked passes. A pass that ticks NOTHING already
ends the loop, so this only bounds slow-but-real progress.
`remediate` sits right after `analyze` and is the one phase that deliberately
drops analyze's own contract. Upstream's /speckit-analyze is STRICTLY READ-ONLY
and ends by ASKING the user to approve remediation edits before anything is
applied — a human-in-the-loop step by design. `remediate` is the touchless
version: it re-runs the same cross-artifact analysis itself (analyze's artifact
is null, so there is no report file on disk for a later process to read — the
handoff between phases is files, and analyze deliberately leaves none) and then
applies the fixes directly to spec.md, plan.md, tasks.md and plan's supporting
design docs (data-model.md, research.md, contracts/, quickstart.md), no approval
step. It is bounded the same way converge is: default write_scope only (specs/,
.specify/), so it can edit those documents but never code, and a finding that is
a genuine product decision — not a documentation defect — is reported as
needs_input rather than resolved by guessing. It writes remediate-report.md as
its artifact, one row per finding, so "nothing was wrong" and "nothing was
checked" stay distinguishable the same way review.md keeps them apart.
It does NOT require `analyze` to have run first in the same invocation —
`--with remediate` alone is the common case, since it performs its own analysis
pass. Requesting both `--with analyze,remediate` still works (analyze produces a
human-readable report first, remediate then re-derives and fixes), at the cost
of running the same detection twice.
`converge` sits BEFORE implement, which is not where its own skill doc puts it
(that says after). The position is chosen for the case it actually gets used in:
an implement phase that died or fell short, where the codebase holds real work
and tasks.md does not know about it. From here, `--resume --with converge` is ONE
command that assesses the code, appends only what is missing, and then finishes
it. After implement it would take two. Measured: a killed implement left 34
modified files that type-checked apart from three unpopulated producers, and 0 of
57 tasks ticked — nothing in tasks.md pointed at the gap. It is opt-in, so an
ordinary run is unaffected, and it gets the DEFAULT write scope (specs/, .specify/)
rather than implement's unrestricted one, because converge appends to tasks.md and
must never write code.
`review` runs AFTER implement and is the only phase that reads code in order to
judge it. Everything else here verifies ARTIFACT SHAPE — present, over the byte
floor, no template markers, boxes ticked — which catches a phase that died and
cannot catch a feature that merely has all its files. The gap it is aimed at is
structural rather than incidental: a chunked implement runs each task group in
its own process and hands off through tasks.md alone, so pass 4 knows only what
pass 2 left on disk. Each pass is individually plausible; nothing had yet read
them side by side. So the defects that reach here are the cross-pass ones — two
passes inventing the same helper twice, a data shape that drifted between
producer and consumer, an obligation every task addressed partially and none
addressed fully.
It is NOT optional, unlike analyze and converge. An opt-in final check is a
check that runs on the days you remember to ask for it, which are not the days
you need it. It gets the default write scope, so it can write review.md and
append remediation tasks but cannot touch code; fixing is implement's job, which
is why findings become tasks. And because review appends to tasks.md, a
`spec-run --resume` after a blocking review re-enters the chunked implement loop
on the new tasks and then reviews again — the remediation loop is the machinery
that already exists, not a new path.
It gates on_needs_input rather than always, and that distinction is load-bearing:
a clean review must pass STRAIGHT THROUGH to the merge stop the roadmap already
owns. Gating always would stop every run to show a human a report saying nothing
is wrong, which is a gate with nothing to decide — the same failure the BLOCKED-
task rule in verify.sh exists to undo. What makes needs_input meaningful here is
that verify.sh reads review.md for UNRESOLVED BLOCKER/MAJOR findings, so the
verdict is the file's state and not the phase's opinion of itself.
implement takes mcp: none, which reverses the earlier default of inherit. Every
MCP tool definition sits in the CACHED PREFIX of every turn, so a phase that
never calls one still pays for the whole list once per turn — and cache reads
are the bulk of a phase's bill (measured across 40 real phase envelopes: 60-75%
cache reads, ~20% cache writes at the 1-hour TTL's doubled rate, 10-15% output).
On a host with a large MCP surface that is the cheapest reduction available,
because it removes a fixed cost paid T times rather than shortening the work.
⚠️ If a project's implement phase genuinely drives an MCP server — a browser, a
deploy API — put it back with `--mcp implement=inherit` or in your own config.
The flag exists so the two can be MEASURED against each other on one feature
rather than argued about: run it both ways and compare cost.log's cache_read.
permission_mode is bypassPermissions, and the reason is measured rather than
assumed. Under acceptEdits (and dontAsk) a Bash command with a LEADING
ENVIRONMENT ASSIGNMENT is denied: `PROBE=1 echo hi` is refused where `echo hi`
is allowed. That is exactly the shape spec-kit's own branch script needs —
`GIT_BRANCH_NAME=... create-new-feature-branch.sh` — so a real specify phase
was refused four times, created no feature branch, and still reported success.
The safety this trades away is less than it looks, and that too was measured:
--disallowed-tools STILL applies under bypassPermissions. `git push` was
blocked with the phase reporting `a permission denial, it did not execute`. So
pushing, merging and deploying remain withheld; what bypass restores is the
ordinary shell the phases need to do their job. `auto` also allows the
env-prefixed form if you prefer a classifier to a rule.
defaults.claude_bin is the executable each phase runs. Point it at a wrapper
(--claude-bin, or SPEC_RUN_CLAUDE_BIN) when the plain CLI cannot get through
your organisation's permission prompts. Whatever you name is probed for the
flags this engine passes, and a flag it does not accept is reported rather
than dropped: a ceiling that was never applied must not read as one that was.

_deny_tools_note: Monitor and TaskOutput are withheld for the same reason as ScheduleWakeup:
a headless phase has nobody to wait for. Measured 2026-09-24: 121 of 1,442
phase sessions backgrounded work and then watched or polled it despite the
handoff telling them to run synchronously. One implement pass (wt-hub-membership
349) wrote its STATUS line, and a Monitor it had armed on a background pytest
then woke it for two more segments at a ~450k-token context. Prose had already
been tried; removing the tool is the structural fix.
deny_tools is a CHEAP EARLY REFUSAL, not the security boundary. Measured
2026-08-24 against the real CLI:
* 'Bash(curl:*)' and 'Bash(source *.env*)' DO refuse the conventional
spelling — permission_denials records the exact command and the phase is
told it did not run, so it stops instead of spending turns on it.
* '/usr/bin/curl ...' EVADES them entirely (0 denials, the command ran).
An absolute path, a shell wrapper or any alternate spelling walks past
every pattern here.
So what actually stopped entry 2's phase from reaching the production context
agent was the SANDBOX (TLS refused, curl exit 60), not this list. Read these
entries as: they make an honest attempt fail fast and legibly. They do not
make egress impossible, and a phase that wants out will get out unless the
sandbox says otherwise.
⚠️ 'Bash(. *.env*)' was REMOVED after one pass in production. It was meant to
catch dot-sourcing a credentials file and instead matched
cd <repo> PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/alembic upgrade head
because `PYTHONPATH=.` ends in a dot, the next word is `.venv/...`, and `.venv`
glob-matches `*.env*`. In a Python repo that is most commands, so the guard
blocked the migrations a phase legitimately needed. 'Bash(source *.env*)' is
kept: `source` is a whole word and cannot collide the same way. The lesson is
that a one-character command name makes a terrible pattern anchor.
